lexemes.note: Zero, the digit and the score. Originally a noun meaning “end, nothing”; it never changes.

override.pos: Wiktionary files אֶפֶס only as a noun (“end; zero (digit)”); in counting, phone numbers and scores it is the numeral zero, so the course files it with the numbers (NUM).

lexemes.note: The only number that comes after the noun and agrees like an adjective: סֵפֶר אֶחָד, מִטָּה אַחַת. The feminine אַחַת is the counting form (אַחַת, שְׁתַּיִם, שָׁלוֹשׁ …).
Before a noun always the construct form: שְׁנֵי סְפָרִים, שְׁתֵּי מִטּוֹת (also before a definite noun: שְׁנֵי הַסְּפָרִים). Alone: שְׁנַיִם / שְׁתַּיִם (counting: שְׁתַּיִם).

With a masculine noun use the form in -ָה (שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים), with a feminine noun the short form (שָׁלוֹשׁ מִטּוֹת) — the reverse of what the endings suggest. Before a definite masculine noun: שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַ… (“the three …”). Counting form: שָׁלוֹשׁ.

With a masculine noun use the form in -ָה (אַרְבָּעָה סְפָרִים), with a feminine noun the short form (אַרְבַּע מִטּוֹת) — the reverse of what the endings suggest. Before a definite masculine noun: אַרְבַּעַת הַ… (“the four …”). Counting form: אַרְבַּע.

With a masculine noun use the form in -ָה (חֲמִשָּׁה סְפָרִים), with a feminine noun the short form (חָמֵשׁ מִטּוֹת) — the reverse of what the endings suggest. Before a definite masculine noun: חֲמֵשֶׁת הַ… (“the five …”). Counting form: חָמֵשׁ.

With a masculine noun use the form in -ָה (שִׁשָּׁה סְפָרִים), with a feminine noun the short form (שֵׁשׁ מִטּוֹת) — the reverse of what the endings suggest. Before a definite masculine noun: שֵׁשֶׁת הַ… (“the six …”). Counting form: שֵׁשׁ.

With a masculine noun use the form in -ָה (שִׁבְעָה סְפָרִים), with a feminine noun the short form (שֶׁבַע מִטּוֹת) — the reverse of what the endings suggest. Before a definite masculine noun: שִׁבְעַת הַ… (“the seven …”). Counting form: שֶׁבַע.

With a masculine noun use the form in -ָה (שְׁמוֹנָה סְפָרִים), with a feminine noun the short form (שְׁמוֹנֶה מִטּוֹת) — the reverse of what the endings suggest. Before a definite masculine noun: שְׁמוֹנַת הַ… (“the eight …”). Counting form: שְׁמוֹנֶה.

override.NUM;FEM;PFX: the form after the prefix מִ, whose נ doubles the first letter (מִשְּׁמוֹנֶה); Wiktionary lists only the plain form.

lexemes.note: With a masculine noun use the form in -ָה (תִּשְׁעָה סְפָרִים), with a feminine noun the short form (תֵּשַׁע מִטּוֹת) — the reverse of what the endings suggest. Before a definite masculine noun: תִּשְׁעַת הַ… (“the nine …”). Counting form: תֵּשַׁע.

With a masculine noun use the form in -ָה (עֲשָׂרָה סְפָרִים), with a feminine noun the short form (עֶשֶׂר מִטּוֹת) — the reverse of what the endings suggest. Before a definite masculine noun: עֲשֶׂרֶת הַ… (“the ten …”). Counting form: עֶשֶׂר.
Masculine with masculine nouns (אַחַד עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (אַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.
Masculine with masculine nouns (שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.
Masculine with masculine nouns (שְׁלוֹשָׁה עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (שְׁלוֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.
Masculine with masculine nouns (אַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (אַרְבַּע עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.
Masculine with masculine nouns (חֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.

override.meaning: The short spelling חמשה עשר has a Wiktionary page that only says “defective spelling of חמישה עשר”, and the check follows just its first word (חמישה “five”); the full page חמישה עשר glosses the word “fifteen”.

lexemes.note: Masculine with masculine nouns (שִׁשָּׁה עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (שֵׁשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.

override.meaning: The short spelling ששה עשר has a Wiktionary page that only says “defective spelling of שישה עשר”, and the check follows just its first word (שישה “six”); the full page שישה עשר glosses the word “sixteen”.

lexemes.note: Masculine with masculine nouns (שִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (שְׁבַע עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.
Masculine with masculine nouns (שְׁמוֹנָה עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (שְׁמוֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.
Masculine with masculine nouns (תִּשְׁעָה עָשָׂר …), feminine with feminine nouns (תְּשַׁע עֶשְׂרֵה …); the noun after it is plural.
The same form for masculine and feminine nouns; 21, 22 … are said ten first: עֶשְׂרִים וְאֶחָד / עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת.
The same form for masculine and feminine nouns; 21, 22 … are said ten first: שְׁלוֹשִׁים וְאֶחָד / שְׁלוֹשִׁים וְאַחַת.
The same form for masculine and feminine nouns; 21, 22 … are said ten first: אַרְבָּעִים וְאֶחָד / אַרְבָּעִים וְאַחַת.
The same form for masculine and feminine nouns; 21, 22 … are said ten first: חֲמִשִּׁים וְאֶחָד / חֲמִשִּׁים וְאַחַת.
The same form for masculine and feminine nouns; 21, 22 … are said ten first: שִׁשִּׁים וְאֶחָד / שִׁשִּׁים וְאַחַת.
The same form for masculine and feminine nouns; 21, 22 … are said ten first: שִׁבְעִים וְאֶחָד / שִׁבְעִים וְאַחַת.
The same form for masculine and feminine nouns; 21, 22 … are said ten first: שְׁמוֹנִים וְאֶחָד / שְׁמוֹנִים וְאַחַת.
The same form for masculine and feminine nouns; 21, 22 … are said ten first: תִּשְׁעִים וְאֶחָד / תִּשְׁעִים וְאַחַת.
Feminine: 200 is the dual מָאתַיִם, 300–900 the feminine number + the plural מֵאוֹת (שְׁלוֹשׁ מֵאוֹת). Alone, מֵאוֹת = “hundreds”.
Masculine: 2000 is the dual אַלְפַּיִם, 3000–9000 the masculine construct + the plural אֲלָפִים (שְׁלוֹשֶׁת אֲלָפִים). Alone, אֲלָפִים = “thousands”.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: Invariable: הַרְבֵּה סְפָרִים, הַרְבֵּה מִטּוֹת, הַרְבֵּה נְיָר — before the noun, no article on the noun.

profile.feeling: Plenty — the everyday “a lot”, for things you count and things you don’t.

senses.def: many, much, a lot of (before a noun)
a lot, much (after a verb or alone)

examples.tr: There were a lot of people there.

synonyms.nuance: “many” as an adjective that agrees (אֲנָשִׁים רַבִּים, שָׁנִים רַבּוֹת) — written and formal style
“loads of” in slang: מָלֵא אֲנָשִׁים “tons of people” (literally “full”)

etymology.text: From the causative (hif‘il) of רָבָה “to be numerous, plentiful”: originally its infinitive absolute, which became an adverb and a determiner.

funFacts: The same Semitic “much, great” is in רַב “great; master” and in רַבִּי “rabbi”, literally “my master”; Arabic رَبّ (rabb) “lord” is its cousin.
pitfalls: הַרְבֵּה never changes: no gender, no plural — הַרְבֵּה סְפָרִים, הַרְבֵּה מִטּוֹת.
It stands before the noun, and the noun has no article: הַרְבֵּה אֲנָשִׁים, not *הַרְבֵּה הָאֲנָשִׁים.
subtleties: One word for English many and much: with a countable noun the noun is plural (הַרְבֵּה סְפָרִים), with a mass noun it stays singular (הַרְבֵּה נְיָר).

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: Invariable, before the noun: מְעַט אֲנָשִׁים “few people”, מְעַט זְמַן “little time”. In casual speech “few” is more often לֹא הַרְבֵּה.

profile.feeling: Not much, not many — a slightly bookish word; in chat people prefer קְצָת or לֹא הַרְבֵּה.

senses.def: few, little (not many, not much) — before a noun

synonyms.nuance: “a little” — the everyday word for an amount (קְצָת נְיָר); it is not used for “few people”
“not many, not much” — the most natural way to say “few” in conversation
“few” as an adjective that agrees: אֲנָשִׁים מְעַטִּים

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology for מְעַט itself; its root מ־ע־ט “to be few” also gives the verb מִעֵט “to diminish” and the noun מִעוּט “minority” (Wiktionary, מִעוּט).

funFacts: כִּמְעַט “almost” and עוֹד מְעַט “soon” are built on it: כְּ “like” + מְעַט “a little”, עוֹד “still” + מְעַט.
pitfalls: מְעַט with a plural noun means “few” (מְעַט אֲנָשִׁים); “a few” (some) is כַּמָּה: כַּמָּה אֲנָשִׁים.
Like הַרְבֵּה it does not change and takes no article on the noun after it.
subtleties: English separates few (count) and little (mass); מְעַט covers both: מְעַט אֲנָשִׁים, מְעַט זְמַן.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: Invariable. Before a mass noun: קְצָת נְיָר “a little / some paper”; before an adjective it softens: קְצָת קָשֶׁה “a bit hard”.

contrasts.value: an amount you do not count (קְצָת לֶחֶם)

profile.feeling: A bit — soft and friendly; Israelis use it all the time, also to soften what they say.

senses.def: some (an amount of something you do not count)
a bit, somewhat (with an adjective or a verb)

synonyms.nuance: the written word for “a little; few”
“a drop” — a tiny bit: טִפָּה חָלָב, טִפָּה עָיֵף

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology. The word belongs with מִקְצָת “part of” (as in the rabbinic rule מִקְצָת הַיּוֹם כְּכֻלּוֹ “part of the day counts as the whole day”) and with קָצֶה “end, edge” (Wiktionary, קָצֶה).

funFacts: Israelis soften requests and opinions with it: קְצָת קָשֶׁה לִי “it’s a bit hard for me” often means “it’s very hard”.
pitfalls: For things you count use כַּמָּה “a few”: כַּמָּה סְפָרִים; קְצָת with a plural noun (קְצָת אֲנָשִׁים) is casual speech.
subtleties: Before an adjective it is an adverb: קְצָת עָיֵף “a bit tired”; before a noun it is “a little / some”.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: Pronounced kol (the vowel is a qamats katan). כָּל + a definite noun = all / the whole (כָּל הַסְּפָרִים, כָּל הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה); כָּל + an indefinite singular = every (כָּל יוֹם). Alone: הַכֹּל “everything”.

contrasts.value: statements and open choices (כָּל אֶחָד, כָּל דָּבָר)

override.pos: Wiktionary files the word as the noun כֹּל “all, whole, entirety” and gives כָּל־ as its construct form; that construct is what stands before a noun (כָּל הַסְּפָרִים, כָּל יוֹם), working as a determiner, so the course files כָּל as DET.

profile.feeling: Everything and everyone — one short word for all, whole and every.

senses.def: all, the whole (before a definite noun): כָּל הַסְּפָרִים “all the books”, כָּל הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה “the whole family”
every, each (before an indefinite singular noun): כָּל יוֹם “every day”
any (in negative or open sentences): כָּל דָּבָר “anything”

examples.tr: The whole family is at home.

phrases.meaning: the start is always the hardest part

synonyms.nuance: “everyone, all of them” — stands alone, without a noun
“whole, complete” — an adjective after the noun: יוֹם שָׁלֵם “a whole day”

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *kʷall- or *kull-; compare Arabic كُلّ (kull), Ge‘ez ኵል (kʷəll), Akkadian kalûm, Classical Syriac ܟܠ (kul). The dictionary form is כֹּל; כָּל (kol) is its construct form, the one used before a noun.

funFacts: Arabic كُلّ (kull) is the same word: كُلّ يَوْم (kull yawm) “every day” = כָּל יוֹם.
pitfalls: Say kol, not kal: the sign under כָּ is a qamats katan (a short o).
כָּל הַיּוֹם “all day” ≠ כָּל יוֹם “every day” — the article changes the meaning.
subtleties: Alone, without a noun, “everything” is הַכֹּל (spelled with holam): הַכֹּל בְּסֵדֶר “everything is fine”.

lexemes.note: כֹּל “all” with a personal ending: כֻּלָּנוּ “all of us”, כֻּלְּכֶם / כֻּלְּכֶן “all of you”, כֻּלָּם / כֻּלָּן “all of them”; כֻּלָּם alone = “everyone”.

contrasts.value: alone, with a personal ending (כֻּלָּם, כֻּלָּנוּ)

profile.feeling: Everybody together — “all of us”, “all of them”.

senses.def: all of them; (כֻּלָּם alone) everyone, everybody
all of us / all of you (כֻּלָּנוּ, כֻּלְּכֶם, כֻּלְּכֶן)

synonyms.nuance: “everyone, each one” — stresses each person separately (singular verb)

etymology.text: A form of כֹּל “all” with the third-person masculine plural possessive ending -ָם: “all of them” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic does the same with كُلّ: كُلُّهُمْ (kulluhum) “all of them” — the same word with the same kind of ending.
pitfalls: A group of only women: כֻּלָּן (הַבָּנוֹת? כֻּלָּן פֹּה). כֻּלָּם is for men or a mixed group.
Everyone is plural in Hebrew: כֻּלָּם פֹּה, כֻּלָּם אוֹהֲבִים — the verb is plural.
subtleties: It can stand after the noun too: הַתַּלְמִידִים כֻּלָּם פֹּה “the students are all here”.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: Invariable, before a plural noun: כַּמָּה סְפָרִים “a few books”. The same word asks “how many / how much?” (lesson 10): only the question shows the difference.

contrasts.value: a few things you count (כַּמָּה סְפָרִים)

profile.feeling: A handful — and the question everybody asks at the market: כַּמָּה?

senses.def: some, a few, several (before a plural noun)

examples.tr: There were a few students here.
How many brothers and sisters do you have?

collocations.tr: how long (how much time); some time

phrases.tr: on one, how much and how much

synonyms.nuance: “a few, several” in writing: סְפָרִים אֲחָדִים
“some” of something you do not count (קְצָת מַיִם); כַּמָּה is for things you count

etymology.text: Wiktionary relates it to Arabic كَمْ (kam) “how many, how much”.

funFacts: Arabic كَمْ (kam) asks “how many?” too — but Arabic keeps the noun singular after it (كَمْ كِتَابًا), while Hebrew makes it plural (כַּמָּה סְפָרִים).
pitfalls: The same word asks and states: כַּמָּה סְפָרִים? “how many books?” — כַּמָּה סְפָרִים. “a few books”. Intonation and the question mark decide.
The noun after it is plural: כַּמָּה יְלָדִים, never *כַּמָּה יֶלֶד.
subtleties: In a question about something you do not count it means “how much”: כַּמָּה זְמַן? “how much time?”
